=== Morphological Assessment Form ===
A. Leaf Arrangement & Architecture
    1. Leaf relative position (alternate / opposite / whorled): alternate (leaves are attached at successive nodes along the stem, alternating sides, as seen in the close-up views)
    2. Leaf spacing (clustered / distal): distal (leaves are spaced out along the stem, not clustered at the apex or base)

B. Leaf Complexity
    3. Leaf complexity (simple / compound): compound (each leaf unit consists of multiple leaflets attached to a central rachis)
    4. Compound leaf type, ONLY if leaf complexity is compound (odd-pinnate / even-pinnate): odd-pinnate (the terminal leaflet is present, and leaflets are arranged along the rachis in pairs with one at the end)
    5. Number of leaflets (integer estimate 2, 4, 8, …): 7 (based on the most clearly visible compound leaf, which has 3 pairs of leaflets plus a terminal leaflet, totaling 7)
    6. Leaflet arrangement (opposite / alternate / subopposite): alternate (leaflets are arranged along the rachis in an alternating pattern, not in direct pairs)

C. Leaf Morphology
    7. Leaf margin (entire / toothed) AND if toothed (dentate, serrate, etc.)): entire (margins are smooth without teeth or serrations, visible in close-up images)
    8. Leaf shape (elliptic, obovate, lanceolate, etc.): lanceolate (leaflets are elongated with a broad base tapering to a pointed tip)
    9. Leaf apex (acute, obtuse, acuminate): acute (tip is sharply pointed but not drawn out into a long tail)
    10. Leaf base (rounded, cordate, cuneate): cuneate (base is wedge-shaped, tapering to the petiole attachment)
    11. Venation type (pinnate / palmate / parallel): pinnate (primary veins extend from the midrib to the margin in a feather-like pattern)
    12. Secondary veins (visibility, spacing, number): visible, closely spaced, numerous (secondary veins are clearly visible and run perpendicular to the midrib, forming a dense network)
    13. Leaf surface features (glabrous, shiny, dull, rugose): shiny (surface has a glossy appearance, reflecting light, especially when wet)
    14. Leaf surface trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs or fuzz on the leaf surface)
    15. Petiole length (short / long): short (petioles are relatively short, connecting leaflets to the rachis without elongation)
    16. Petiole features (winged / grooved / terete): terete (petioles are round in cross-section, without wings or grooves)

D. Stem & Shoot Traits
    17. Stem type, may not be visible (woody / herbaceous): herbaceous (stem appears green and flexible, typical of young seedlings; not woody)
    18. Stem trichomes (present / absent): absent (no visible hairs or trichomes on the stem surface)
    19. Stem color: green (stem is uniformly green, consistent across all images)
    20. Stem texture (smooth / ridged / lenticellate): smooth (surface is even without ridges or lenticels)

E. Other Visible Seedling Traits
    21. Stipules, sometimes visible only in close-up images (present / absent): absent (no stipules observed at leaf bases in any image)
    22. Latex, rarely visible but extremely diagnostic when present (present / not observed): not observed (no latex exudate visible from stem or leaves)
    23. Pulvinus, for Fabaceae family only (present / absent): absent (no visible pulvinus at leaflet or leaf base; not applicable if not Fabaceae, but assessed as absent)
    24. Tendrils (present / absent): absent (no tendrils observed on any part of the seedling)

F. Notes: Some leaves show minor damage such as holes and marginal tearing, likely from mechanical or environmental causes. Trees, climbing shrubs, or lianas; stipules absent. Leaves compound, odd-pinnate or trifoliate, indumentum of simple trichomes, the blade sometimes with glandular dots on the underside, margin entire; petiole and petiolules pulvinated. Inflorescences in panicles, racemes, or spike-like, axillary or terminal. Flowers bisexual, white, yellowish, or pale pink; sepals 5, valvate or imbricate; petals 5, free; stamens 10, forming a short tube at the base; ovary superior, carpels 1-5, style one per carpel; ovules 2 per carpel. Fruit in follicles, often red; seeds 1 per fruit, black, the aril bright red, yellow, white, or orange.
The family consists of 16 genera and about 300–350 species, pantropical, with a distribution center in western Africa; for tropical America, 5 genera and 108 species are known; 3 genera and 9 species in CR.
It is characterized by its compound leaves, mainly trifoliate or odd-pinnate, leaflets alternate on the rachis, sometimes with dendritic trichomes, petioles clearly pulvinated, stipules absent, and the fruit follicles with a black seed with a reddish basal aril. In vegetative form, its general appearance relates it directly to the family Fabaceae, but several of the characteristics mentioned earlier allow it to be separated.
Traditionally, the family has been placed within the Order Rosales, or in close relation to the Order Sapindales, and some have suggested a link between such Orders. However, recent molecular studies suggest that its placement is in the Order Oxalidales, along with families such as: Oxalidaceae, Cunnoniaceae, Elaeocarpaceae, etc.

Adult plants frequent in the forest; seedlings common and recognizable by the large orbicular fimbriate stipules. Flowers in the late rainy season (August to November). The fruits mature within 1 month. Costa Rica to Peru and Brazil. In Panama, known from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Colon and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone (Pipeline Road), Veraguas, and Panama (Cerro Jefe). [Paullinia turbacensis] is a tendriled liana; stems terete, ± glabrous, bearing conspicuous brown lenticels; sap at periphery milky, not copious. Leaves trifoliolate; petioles to 14 cm long, with marginal ribs above, glabrate; leaflets broadly elliptic, acuminate or acute at apex, attenuate to rounded at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-12 cm wide (to 23 cm long and 11 cm wide as juveniles), glabrate but with axillary tufts below, subentire to remotely crenate-dentate. Thyrses small, helicoid, to 7 cm long, solitary or clustered at nodes, often on leafless stems near the ground but occurring to 5 m high; flowers white, ca 5 mm long; petals with the scales ca two-thirds as long as petals, yellow-crested, the anterior scales bilobed, their appendages pubescent, the glands white, acute, densely pubescent; staminal cluster equaling petals; filaments densely pubescent; nectar abundant, stored near the large glands; ovary glabrous; styles pubescent. Capsules elliptic to obovate, 2 cm long, red, short-pubescent, the 3 boat-shaped valves broadly spreading to expose seeds; seeds 1-3, black, shiny, less than 1 cm long, covered on the lower half by a fleshy white aril, dangling on a thin funiculus when fully displayed.

Tree, to 30 m tall and 40 cm dbh (often much shorter along the shore); outer bark hard, closely fissured; inner bark red; younger stems, leaf rachises, and axes of inflorescences densely strigose and puberulent (in Panama) or sparsely strigose, sparsely puberulent, or nearly glabrous (often in South America). Leaves alternate, imparipinnate, mostly 15-30 cm long; petioles flat on upper surface with marginal ribs; leaflets apparently never dimorphic, usually 5-9 (rarely 3 or 10), usually alternate, ± elliptic, acuminate, obtuse-attenuate at base, 4-21 cm long, 1.5-8 cm wide, usually glabrous or minutely puberulent and/or strigose on midrib on both surfaces, rarely strigose below; midrib sharply raised. Panicles axillary (often appearing terminal), mostly 8-20 cm long; flowers white or greenish-yellow, 4-6-parted, as wide as long, globular in bud, the trichomes (at least on calyx) erect or appressed; calyx saucer-shaped, the lobes acute or blunt; petals valvate, ovate, to ca 2 mm long, glabrous or sparsely appressed-pubescent outside, glabrous inside, the margins papillose-puberulent; staminal tube two-thirds to three-fourths as long as petals, broader than long, glabrous outside and in but sometimes pubescent inside near apex, the lobes narrowly acute; anthers twice as many as petals, very narrowly ovoid, ca 0.5 mm long, alternating with and usually longer than lobes of staminal tube; ovary broadly ovoid, densely appressed-pubescent with white trichomes all over; style usually glabrous. Capsules ellipsoid, 11-18 mm long, orange at maturity, prominently tuberculate, the 3 (4) valves folding back to expose shiny red aril; seeds 1 or 2, smooth, ellipsoid, ca 1 cm long. Abundant as seedlings; common as adults in the forest, especially in the old forest. Flowering is bimodal, but principally from April to June, especially in June; a second but much smaller flowering period may occur from September to November. [unclear reference] The fruits from the first flowering mature mostly during September and October, especially in October; mature fruits from the second flowering have been seen in June.

Tree, 4.5-35 m, the young twigs minutely adpressed-pubescent to glabrescent. Leaves with the petiole 0.5-1.2 cm; blade 10-30 X 3.5-12 cm, elliptical to oblong-elliptical, acute to obtuse or (rarely) subtruncate at the base, glabrous on the underside, without domatia or (rarely) with countable trichomes in the axils of the main veins, with (4)5-8 secondary veins on each side. Inflorescences [of Nectandra purpurea] 10-17 cm. Flowers with the tepals (1—)1.2—2(—2.4) mm. Fruits 1-1.5 cm, ellipsoidal; cup ca. 0.3 cm. Very wet and pluvial forest, 0-1550 m; Caribbean [vertical] Cords. of Guanacaste, Triarán and Central (E.B. La Selva), San Carlos and Tortuguero Plains, Low Talamanca, both [vertical] Cord. de Talamanca, [Pacific] vertical, S Coastal Range (Fila Cruces). Flowers [of Nectandra purpurea] May-Sept. [in Nicaragua, Bolivia] and [Venezuela], [in the] Guiana [region], [in] Brazil. (Grayum et al. 8898, MO) Nectandra purpurea is recognized by its leaf blades that dry relatively opaque on the adaxial side, with the secondary veins slightly elevated and interconnected, forming a submarginal vein and by its flowers with the tepals densely covered by brown or yellowish trichomes and (usually) with the staminodes conspicuously elevated. The cupules that dry light brown, ± puberulent, are also distinctive.

Androdioecious liana or scandent shrub; young stems, petioles, and axes of inflorescences with moderate to dense stellate pubescence interspersed with simple trichomes. Petioles 3-10 mm long, winged full length; blades elliptic to obovate, rounded to abruptly acuminate (rarely short-acuminate), acute to obtuse and decurrent on petiole at base, 5-18 cm long, 3-8 cm wide, the pubescence minute, pustular, stellate on both surfaces, the simple trichomes mostly restricted to veins; lateral veins in 15-25 pairs. Panicles spikelike; flowers unisexual, usually subsessile, 4-5 mm broad, closely congested; sepals 5; petals (2)3(4), pale yellow to greenish-white, rounded at apex, soon falling, the margin folded inward; stamens numerous, to ca 5 mm long, reduced in pistillate flowers; pistils reduced in staminate flowers; style usually directed to one side; stigma ± spatulate-truncate. Follicle 1, glabrous, shiny, dark brown, 5-7 mm long (excluding prominent beak), dehiscing on one side from style downward to expose seed; seeds 1-4, shiny, black, 3-4 mm long, enveloped at least in part by a deeply lacerate red aril. Frequent along the shore and in the forest. Flowering may be induced throughout much of the year, but the chief flowering period is the early dry season (December to March, especially January and February). Flowering appears to be induced by drought. Severing a vine in the proper stage of bud will soon cause the flowers to open. The fruits mature mostly from March to May (sometimes from February). Mexico to Colombia.

Locating an individual
It is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Distribution
From Belize to Venezuela, the Guianas, Brazil, and Bolivia. In Costa Rica, it is widely distributed in the medium to low elevations of both slopes, in climates ranging from humid to very humid, although it prefers climates with marked seasonality; 0-700-800 m.
Habit
Trees, 15-35 m tall.
Trunk
Trunk with reddish-brown outer bark.
Bark
Outer bark reddish-brown, scaly, inner bark reddish with a pleasant mango scent; white or milky resinous sap.
Leaves
Odd-pinnate leaves, with 7-9 leaflets, elliptical, oblong, or oblong-lanceolate, 5-21 x 4-7.2 cm, apex acuminate to abruptly acuminate, base obtuse to asymmetric, generally glabrous; petiolules without evident pulvini, margin entire; petioles 4-14 cm long.
Flowers
Inflorescences are panicles, 3-15 cm long, axillary. Yellowish or greenish-yellow flowers (unisexual); calyx with 5 lobes, 1-1.5 mm long, cuculiform; petals (tubular corolla), with 5 lobes, 5-5.5 mm long; stamens 10, 1 mm long, filaments inserted at the base of the disc; annular disc with 10 lobes; ovary with 5 lobes, ovoid, with 5 locules; style 1, stigma with 5 lobes.
Fruits
Capsular and drupe-like fruits, 1.5-2.5 x 1.5 x 3 cm, ovoid or more or less turbinate, with 2-5 lobes, dehiscent by 4-5 valves, scarlet red inside, red to black when mature; pyrenes 3-5, 12-13 mm thick, white, the mesocarp (pseudoaril) reddish turning white upon exposure (dehiscence), fleshy, juicy, sweet, and edible.
Diagnosis
Characterized by being a large tree, the bark on mature trees is somewhat scaly, lenticellate, and the inner bark has a very particular and pleasant mango scent. At the vegetative level, it is sometimes confused with the genus Protium, although its leaves lack pulvinated petiolules and the turpentine aroma when crushed. Its fruits are distinctive for their peculiar turbinate shape.
Habitat
In the Forest; it is mainly observed towards the Southern Boundary (LS), Quebrada El Salto, etc., in rolling or broken terrain.
Phenology
Flowers observed in June and August; fruits in August and February.

Tree, 3.5-11 (13) m tall; trunk usually 6-15 cm dbh; bark with moderately close, deep vertical fissures, but not flaking; young stems, axes of inflorescences, petioles, and underside of veins densely rufous-pubescent, the trichomes pinnately branched, often somewhat stalked. Petioles to 9 cm long; blades broadly elliptic, obtuse to abruptly short-acuminate, obtuse to rounded at base, 9-35 cm long, 6-18 cm wide, denticulate, the surface below canescent and completely covered with trichomes, these sessile, stellate, in part with a brown center; veins 5, dark. Panicles large, terminal, 18-22 cm long, branched many times, the branches ± flattened or angulate; flowers ± sessile; hypanthium and calyx together 1.5-2 mm long, campanulate, the teeth obscure or lacking; petals 5, white, obovate, to 1.5 mm long. Berries round to depressedglobose, to 6 mm diam, white to lavender-blue, probably becoming purple-black at full maturity; seeds numerous, minute. Croat 5693, 15070. Known only from shoreline north of the dock and south of Fairchild Point, but undoubtedly more abundant. Seasonal behavior uncertain. Flowers at least in January, February, and May. Mature fruits have been seen in April, May, and October. Easily confused with Miconia argentea, which is similar in most respects except pubescence, trunk bark, and stature. The species ranges from Mexico to Panama and Venezuela; West Indies. In Panama, the species is known only from tropical moist forest in the Canal Zone and Panama and from premontane wet forest in the Canal Zone.

Trees (CR) or shrubs; twigs often quadrangular and sometimes with glands (Qualea); stipules present, 4 or more per node. Leaves simple, opposite or whorled, margin entire. Inflorescences racemose, paniculate or thyrsoid, terminal or axillary. Flowers bisexual, zygomorphic; sepals 5, connate at the base, imbricate, unequal, 1 generally spurred at the base; petals 1–3 (–5); stamens 1–5 (–7), generally with 1 fertile stamen; ovary superior, 3-carpellate, 3-locular, axial placentation. Fruit a loculicidal capsule, trivalvate (except Erisma, 1-locular indehiscent capsule); seeds often winged (except Erisma, linear).
The family consists of 7 genera and around 200 species, neotropical (except Erismadelphus which is African); 2 genera and 5 species in CR; 2 genera and 3 species in LS.
In general, the family is characterized by mainly containing tree species, with simple leaves, opposite or sometimes whorled, conspicuous stipules 4 or more per node, yellow, orange, or pink flowers emerging in racemiform inflorescences that stand out and cover the crown during flowering, making them conspicuous from a distance, and by their dry, trivalvate capsule fruits with winged seeds. The genus Erisma is also exceptional for its inferior ovary position, indehiscent fruit, and the indumentum of star-shaped trichomes.

Fruit a loculicidal capsule, trivalvate (except Erisma, 1-locular indehiscent capsule); seeds often winged (except Erisma, linear).

The genus Erisma is also exceptional for its inferior ovary position, indehiscent fruit, and the indumentum of star-shaped trichomes.

Shrub or small tree, 1-4 m, moderately to densely covered with flexuous, hooked or feathery trichomes, hyaline, and moderately intermixed with tiny, oblong glands, on young twigs, petioles, primary veins raised on the undersides of leaves and [inflorescences]. Leaves 10—29(—39) X (6—)11-21.5 cm, broadly elliptical to elliptical-ovate, broadly rounded and obliquely cordate at the base, shortly acuminate at the apex, inconspicuously wavy-denticulate, glabrous on the adaxial surface, moderately covered on the abaxial surface with a mixture of simple, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes on the secondary and higher order veins, palmately 5-7-nerved. [Inflorescences] with bracteoles 0.5-1 mm, subulate, persistent. [Flowers] with pedicel 1.5-2.5 mm, 5-merous, the hypanthium sparsely covered with a mixture of star-shaped, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes; calyx with lobes 0.25-0.5 mm, wavy and apiculate, the external teeth ca. 0.25 mm, not projecting beyond the lobes, tuberculate; petals white or pale pink, 2.5—4(—5) X 1.5(—3) mm, obovate-oblong, glabrous; anthers yellow, subequal, 1.5-2 mm, oblong, bilocular, with a truncate to retuse pore, the connective without appendage; ovary ca. 3/4 inferior, 5-locular, apex sparsely glandular-pubescent, without a neck; style 3-4 mm, glabrous; stigma not expanded. [Fruits] black purple at maturity, 5-6 X 5-6 mm; seeds 0.5-0.75 mm, broadly deltoid in outline, rounded-angled, smooth, the raphe extended on all sides to form a swollen edge, like a wing. Wet and very wet forest, riverbanks, 50-700 m; Caribbean slope. [The Cordillera de Talamanca], San Carlos Plain, Pacific slope, [the northern part of the Costeña Range (Fila Tinamastes)], [the southern part of the Nicoya Peninsula], [the protected area of P.N. Carara], regions of Puriscal and Golfo Dulce. Fl. Apr., Jul., Aug., Nov., Dec. [Miconia simplex is] recognized by its large leaves, broadly rounded to obliquely cordate at the base and shortly acuminate at the apex, the connective of the anthers without appendage, the ovary 5-locular, and the seeds with an inflated wing-like margin.

Shrub or small tree, 1-4 m, moderately to densely covered with flexuous, hooked or feathery trichomes, hyaline, and moderately intermixed with tiny, oblong glands, on young twigs, petioles, primary veins raised on the undersides of leaves and inflorescences. Leaves 10—29(—39) X (6—)11-21.5 cm, broadly elliptical to elliptical-ovate, broadly rounded and obliquely cordate at the base, shortly acuminate at the apex, inconspicuously wavy-denticulate, glabrous on the adaxial surface, moderately covered on the abaxial surface with a mixture of simple, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes on the secondary and higher order veins, palmately 5-7-nerved. Inflorescences with bracteoles 0.5-1 mm, subulate, persistent. Flowers with pedicel 1.5-2.5 mm, 5-merous, the hypanthium sparsely covered with a mixture of star-shaped, hooked and tiny, glandular trichomes; calyx with lobes 0.25-0.5 mm, wavy and apiculate, the external teeth ca. 0.25 mm, not projecting beyond the lobes, tuberculate; petals white or pale pink, 2.5—4(—5) X 1.5(—3) mm, obovate-oblong, glabrous; anthers yellow, subequal, 1.5-2 mm, oblong, bilocular, with a truncate to retuse pore, the connective without appendage; ovary ca. 3/4 inferior, 5-locular, apex sparsely glandular-pubescent, without a neck; style 3-4 mm, glabrous; stigma not expanded. Fruits black purple at maturity, 5-6 X 5-6 mm; seeds 0.5-0.75 mm, broadly deltoid in outline, rounded-angled, smooth, the raphe extended on all sides to form a swollen edge, like a wing. Very wet forest, riverbanks, 50-700 m; Caribbean slope. Cordillera de Talamanca, San Carlos Plain, Pacific slope, Northern Costeña Range (Fila Tinamastes), Southern Nicoya Peninsula, Parque Nacional Carara, regions of Puriscal and Golfo Dulce. Flowers April, July, August, November, December. Miconia simplex is recognized by its large leaves, broadly rounded to obliquely cordate at the base and shortly acuminate at the apex, the connective of the anthers without appendage, the ovary 5-locular, and the seeds with an inflated wing-like margin.

Dioecious shrub or tree, to 15 m tall; trunk slender or to 20 cm dbh and deeply invaginated; stems sericeous when very young, glabrate in age, with conspicuous leaf scars. Leaves somewhat clustered at apex of branchlets; stipules caducous, to 1 cm long, sericeous, leaving a conspicuous interpetiolar line of trichomes; petioles 6-14 mm long, sericeous to glabrate; blades ovate-elliptic to obovate-elliptic, abruptly short-acuminate, usually obtuse and ± decurrent onto petiole at base, 7-13(21) cm long, 3.5-8 (12) cm wide, glabrous or with sparse long trichomes on major veins below and tufts of trichomes in axils, the margins ciliate and ± revolute.

Dioecious, hemiepiphytic tree, to 10 m tall; trunk to 15 cm dbh; branches spiraled, stiff and spreading, densely rooting at the nodes, the roots often extending back to the host tree and enveloping the host tree for support; stems glabrous with prominent leaf scars; sap pale yellow to bright orange (in time), not copious. Petioles to 2 cm long; blades obovate, rounded at apex (sometimes acute to acuminate on juvenile leaves), acute to obtuse at base, 5-15 cm long, 3-10 cm wide, very thick, dark green and glossy above, dull below, coriaceous; veins indistinct, drying with many fine veins.
